title: Compactness by open covers
objectives: Prove a set is compact with open covers, and prove Heine-Borel on the line.

screens.title: The fewest intervals
screens.prose: Six open intervals lie over $[0, 1]$, the thick bar on the axis. Together they cover it: every point of $[0, 1]$ is in at least one.
screens.question: Tap the fewest intervals that still cover $[0, 1]$.

hints.text: Which intervals contain 0?
Only $I_1$ holds 0, and only $I_3$ holds 1.
Then only $I_2$ holds 0.35.

feedback.correct: Right. Three intervals, and no smaller set works.

byKey.I4: $I_4 = (0.1, 0.32)$ lies inside $I_1$, so it adds nothing.
byKey.I5: $I_5$ lies inside $I_2$, so it adds nothing.
byKey.I6: $I_6$ lies inside $I_2$, so it adds nothing.
byKey.I2: Without $I_2$ the point 0.35 is uncovered: it is not in $I_1 = (-0.1, 0.35)$.

explain.text: Only $I_1$ holds 0, only $I_2$ holds 0.35, and only $I_3$ holds 0.65. So any subcover needs all three, and $\{I_1, I_2, I_3\}$ is the unique smallest.

screens.title: A cover with no finite subcover
screens.prose: An **open cover** of $K$ is a family of open sets whose union contains $K$. A **subcover** is part of it that still covers. $K$ is **compact** when every open cover has a finite subcover. Cover the open disc by $B_2(0, 1 - \tfrac1n)$, $n \ge 2$.
screens.question: Why does no finite subcover exist?

options.text: Finitely many balls are nested; their union is the largest, $B_2(0, 1 - \tfrac1N)$, which misses points near the rim.
The cover has infinitely many members, so any subcover does too.
options.why: A subcover may drop members. The point is that every finite choice leaves a gap.

options.text: The balls never cover the rim.
options.why: The rim is not in the open disc, so it need not be covered.

hints.text: Pick finitely many balls. Which is largest?
The point $(1 - \tfrac{1}{2N}, 0)$ is outside $B_2(0, 1 - \tfrac1N)$.

feedback.correct: Right. So the open disc is not compact.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take any finite choice and find a point it misses.

explain.text: The balls grow with $n$, so a finite choice is just its largest ball $B_2(0, 1 - \tfrac1N)$. It misses $(1 - \tfrac{1}{2N}, 0)$, which lies in the disc. `analysis` l24 did the same with $(\tfrac1n, 1)$ on the line.

screens.title: $[0, 1]$ is compact
screens.prose: Let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $[0, 1]$. Put $c = \sup S$, where $S = \{x \in [0, 1] : [0, x] \text{ has a finite subcover}\}$. One line is tempting but flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: $0 \in S$, since one member holds 0; so $S$ is non-empty and $c$ exists, by completeness.
Some member $U \in \mathcal{U}$ holds $c$, and $U \supseteq (c - \delta, c + \delta)$ for some $\delta > 0$, as $U$ is open.
Pick $x \in S$ with $x > c - \delta$. A finite subcover of $[0, x]$ plus $U$ covers $[0, \min(c + \tfrac\delta2, 1)]$.
So $\min(c + \tfrac\delta2, 1) \in S$. As $c$ is the supremum, this forces $c = 1$ and $1 \in S$. $\blacksquare$
Pick one member round each point of $[0, 1]$ and keep them all.
lines.why: That gives a subcover, but it may have infinitely many members. Compactness needs a finite one.

hints.text: The member holding $c$ reaches a little past $c$.
Non-empty $S$, the member at $c$, extend the cover, conclude $c = 1$.

feedback.correct: Right. The member at $c$ pushes past the supremum.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Start with why $S$ has a supremum.

byKey.d1: You kept a member for every point. That can be infinitely many, so it is no finite subcover.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: The member $U$ holding $c$ contains an interval round it. Adding $U$ to a finite subcover of $[0, x]$ reaches past $c$ unless $c = 1$. So $[0, 1]$ itself has a finite subcover.

screens.title: Closed inside compact
screens.prose: Let $K$ be compact and $F \subseteq K$ closed. We show $F$ is compact.
screens.question: Put the proof in order.

lines.text: Let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $F$.
$F^c$ is open, so $\mathcal{U} \cup \{F^c\}$ is an open cover of $K$.
$K$ is compact, so finitely many of these sets cover $K$.
Drop $F^c$, which holds no point of $F$: the rest are finitely many members of $\mathcal{U}$ covering $F$. $\blacksquare$

hints.text: Add one open set to cover the rest of $K$.
The complement of $F$ is open because $F$ is closed.

feedback.correct: Right. The complement fills the gap, then leaves.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Extend the cover to all of $K$ first.

explain.text: Adding the open set $F^c$ covers $K$, whose finite subcover may use $F^c$. Removing it still covers $F$. So closed subsets of compact sets are compact.

screens.title: Compact sets are closed
screens.prose: Let $K$ be compact in a metric space and $p \notin K$. We find a ball round $p$ missing $K$. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: The sets $U_n = \{x : d(x, p) > \tfrac1n\}$ are open, and their union is everything except $p$.
So they cover $K$, and by compactness finitely many do; as they grow with $n$, one $U_N$ covers $K$.
Then every point of $K$ is more than $\tfrac1N$ from $p$.
So $B(p, \tfrac1N)$ misses $K$. Every outside point has such a ball, so $K^c$ is open and $K$ is closed. $\blacksquare$
A compact set holds all its limits, so it is closed.
lines.why: That is what we are proving. Here the proof goes through covers, not sequences.

hints.text: Cover $K$ by complements of shrinking closed balls round $p$.
Finitely many nested sets have a largest.

feedback.correct: Right. A compact set keeps its distance from outside points.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Start from the sets $U_n$.

byKey.d1: You assumed the conclusion. The proof must build the ball round $p$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: The complements of the closed balls $\{d(x, p) \le \tfrac1n\}$ cover $K$, and one of them suffices. So $K$ stays $\tfrac1N$ away from $p$, and $K^c$ is open. Covering by $B(x_0, n)$ shows $K$ is bounded in the same way.

screens.title: Heine-Borel on the line
screens.prose: **Heine-Borel:** a subset $K$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded. Two lines may come in either order.
screens.question: Put both directions in order.

lines.text: Let $K$ be compact. The intervals $(-n, n)$ cover $K$; finitely many do, so $K \subseteq (-N, N)$ is bounded.
$K$ is closed, by the last screen.
Conversely let $K$ be closed and bounded, so $K \subseteq [-M, M]$ for some $M$.
$[-M, M]$ is compact, by the proof for $[0, 1]$ rescaled; $K$ is a closed subset, so $K$ is compact. $\blacksquare$

hints.text: Forward: bounded, then closed. Backward: inside an interval.
Closed inside compact is compact.

feedback.correct: Right. Every piece was proved on an earlier screen.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Prove compact gives closed and bounded first.

explain.text: Compact gives bounded by the cover $(-n, n)$ and closed by the last screen. Closed and bounded puts $K$ inside a compact $[-M, M]$ as a closed subset. `analysis` l24 stated this with its idea; here every step is proved.

screens.title: A Lebesgue number
screens.prose: For the hook's cover $I_1, I_2, I_3$ of $[0, 1]$, a **Lebesgue number** is an $L > 0$ with this property. Every subset of $[0, 1]$ of diameter below $L$ lies in one member. Slide a window along $[0, 1]$.
screens.question: What is the largest Lebesgue number of this cover?

hints.text: The tight spots are where one member hands over to the next.
$I_1$ and $I_2$ overlap in $(0.3, 0.35)$.
A set of diameter below 0.05 near 0.3 fits in $I_1$ or $I_2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Measure the overlaps between neighbours.

byKey.radius: 0.025 is the matching ball radius: a ball of radius below 0.025 has diameter below 0.05.
byKey.short: 0.35 is the length of $I_2$. The overlap, not a member, sets the number.

explain.text: A window of width $L$ near 0.3 must fit in $I_1$ or $I_2$, which needs $L \le 0.05$. The same holds near 0.6. So the largest Lebesgue number is 0.05, and every ball of radius below 0.025 lies in one member.

screens.title: One set covers it
screens.prose: A learner says: "$(0, 1)$ is compact. The single open set $(0, 1)$ covers it, and that is a finite subcover."
screens.question: What is wrong with the argument?

options.text: Compact needs a finite subcover of every open cover. The cover by $(\tfrac1n, 1)$ has none.
Nothing: one cover with a finite subcover is enough.
options.why: You swapped the quantifiers, as in `proof` l4. "Every cover has a finite subcover" is not "some cover is finite".
In a discrete space every finite set is open and compact.

hints.text: Read the definition's quantifier: every cover.
Try the cover $(\tfrac1n, 1)$.
Finitely many members reach down only to $\tfrac1N$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The definition quantifies over all open covers.

byKey.fine: You checked one cover. Compactness needs every open cover, and $(\tfrac1n, 1)$ fails.

explain.text: Every set is covered by itself, so that test is empty. The cover $(\tfrac1n, 1)$ has no finite subcover: the largest of finitely many misses $(0, \tfrac1N]$. So $(0, 1)$ is not compact.

screens.title: A convergent sequence with its limit
screens.prose: Take $K = \{0\} \cup \{1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots\}$ and any open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of $K$.
screens.question: Why does $\mathcal{U}$ have a finite subcover?

options.text: The member $U_0$ holding 0 holds all but finitely many $\tfrac1n$; one more member for each of those finishes.
$K$ is closed, and closed sets are compact.
options.why: $\mathbb{R}$ is closed and not compact. $K$ is closed and bounded, and the cover argument shows why.

options.text: $K$ is countable, and countable sets are compact.
options.why: $\mathbb{N}$ is countable and not compact: the cover by $(n - \tfrac12, n + \tfrac12)$ has no finite subcover.

hints.text: Start with a member that holds 0.
$U_0$ contains an interval round 0.
That interval holds every $\tfrac1n$ with $n$ large.

feedback.correct: Right. A sequence with its limit is compact.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the member that holds the limit 0.

explain.text: $U_0 \supseteq (-r, r)$ catches every $\tfrac1n < r$. The finitely many points left each need one member. A finite set is compact the same way: one member per point.

screens.title: A smallest subcover by machine
screens.prose: Write `smallest_subcover(intervals, a, b)`. Start at $x = a$ and take the open interval holding $x$ that reaches furthest. Move $x$ to its right end, and stop once past $b$. Return the sorted indices, or `None` if some $x$ lies in no interval. `Fraction` ends must work exactly.
screens.question: Complete the function.

widget.prelude: from fractions import Fraction as F
widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests, compared exactly. They use the hook, a gap at 0.5 and a cover where greedy needs four. Two have Fraction ends, and one of those leaves $\tfrac13$ uncovered. The last two are one wide interval and a cover missing the end 0. The first Check starts Python in the browser, about 4 s once.

hints.text: Open intervals: test `lo < x < hi`, strictly.
The right end of the chosen interval is not in it, so the next interval must hold that end.

feedback.correct: Right. Greedy reach gives a smallest cover.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use strict inequalities and stop once past $b$.

explain.text: Each step covers $[x, hi)$ and moves to $hi$, which the next interval must contain. Greedy reach is optimal: after $k$ picks it reaches at least as far as any $k$ intervals can. Checking cases is evidence, not proof.

screens.title: A finite scenario grid
screens.prose: Over market moves from $-10\%$ to $10\%$, a book's P&L changes by at most £20,000 per 1% move. A risk system checks finitely many scenarios, every 0.5%. Each move then lies within 0.25% of a grid point.

state.caption: Grid points at every 0.5%, from −10% to 10%.

screens.question: Fill in the grid size and the error bound.

rows: how far the true worst loss can exceed the grid's (£)

hints.text: From $-10$ to 10 in steps of 0.5, count both ends.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the grid points, then multiply the half-step by the rate.

byKey.fence: You counted the gaps. A fence of 40 gaps has 41 posts.
byKey.full: £10,000 uses the full 0.5% step. The nearest grid point is at most half a step away.

explain.text: There are $\tfrac{20}{0.5} + 1 = 41$ scenarios, and every move is within 0.25% of one, so the P&L is within £5,000. The 41 open balls of radius 0.3% round the grid points are a finite subcover of the scenario interval. Compactness is why a finite grid can be enough.

ideas: A set is compact when every open cover has a finite subcover. The open disc and $(0, 1)$ are not; $[0, 1]$ is, by a supremum argument.
Closed subsets of compact sets are compact, and compact sets in a metric space are closed and bounded. Together these give Heine-Borel on $\mathbb{R}$: compact means closed and bounded.
A finite set, and a convergent sequence with its limit, are compact. Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: 0.05 for the hook's cover.

formula.name: Heine-Borel on the line
formula.tex: K \subseteq \mathbb{R} \text{ compact} \iff K \text{ closed and bounded}
formula.note: In $\mathbb{R}^n$ the same holds; in a general metric space only the forward direction.

summary.trap: "$(0, 1)$ covers itself" is no proof of compactness: every open cover must have a finite subcover, and $(\tfrac1n, 1)$ has none.

options.why: Not closed: the cover $[0, 1 - \tfrac1n)$, open in it, has no finite subcover.
Closed but unbounded: the cover by $(n - \tfrac12, n + \tfrac12)$ has no finite subcover.

explain.text: $[0, 1] \cup [2, 3]$ is closed and bounded, so compact by Heine-Borel. $[0, 1)$ is not closed and $\mathbb{N}$ is not bounded.

quiz.prose: A cover of $[0, 1]$ has Lebesgue number 0.05.
quiz.question: Below what radius is every ball $B(x, r)$, $x \in [0, 1]$, sure to lie in one member?

widget.accept: 0.025: a ball of radius $r$ has diameter at most $2r$.

feedback.correct: Right. Radius is half the diameter.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Relate the radius to the diameter.

byKey.same: 0.05 bounds the diameter. A ball's diameter can be twice its radius.

explain.text: A ball of radius $r$ has diameter at most $2r$. So $r < 0.025$ keeps the diameter below 0.05.

quiz.prose: Let $K = \{x_1, \dots, x_m\}$ be a finite subset of any topological space.
quiz.question: Why is $K$ compact?

options.text: From any open cover, pick one member holding each $x_k$: at most $m$ members.
Finite sets are closed, and closed sets are compact.
options.why: Closed sets need not be compact ($\mathbb{R}$), and finite sets need not be closed (Sierpiński).

options.text: Finite sets are bounded, and bounded sets are compact.
options.why: $(0, 1)$ is bounded and not compact; and a topological space may have no metric.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Build the finite subcover directly.

explain.text: Each point lies in some member of the cover. Choosing one for each of the $m$ points gives a subcover of at most $m$ sets.
